entries.name: Generalized Expectation Maximization
entries.definition: A latent-variable likelihood-fitting framework that computes the expected complete-data log likelihood under the current exact posterior and replaces full maximization with a parameter update that does not decrease that same expected objective.
entries.identity_notes: GEM generalizes the M-step requirement of ordinary EM; it does not license an arbitrary approximate E-step. Exact EM and suitable fixed-Q ECM updates are special cases. Cached-case incremental EM, Monte Carlo approximations and ECME actual-likelihood steps do not automatically satisfy the current-Q GEM inequality. The source-defined framework is distinct from any particular gradient, coordinate or space-alternating implementation. Bare GEM is not asserted as a globally unique alias. ECM, AECM and SAGE specialize parameter/augmentation updates, not these case or probability-subset operations. Structured factorial-HMM variational inference imposes a different family restriction. evidence_sources.version: Official NIPS1994 proceedings PDF, Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems7, pp.545-552, published1995. claims.statement: At fixed beta>0 define f_beta(z|x,theta)=p(x,z|theta)^beta/Z_beta(x,theta), where Z is a positive finite latent sum or integral. The power applies to the whole joint density, including mixing weights. Compute expectations under f_beta at the current parameters, then maximize the expected complete log likelihood with that distribution held fixed. Repeat the deterministic stage updates to the chosen stopping condition, increase beta, and warm-start the next stage. Explicitly fit at beta=1 to recover the ordinary EM endpoint.

At fixed beta, the entropy-weighted variational objective profiles to (1/beta)*sum_i log Z_beta(x_i,theta), the negative of the paper’s free energy. Exact admissible coordinate updates increase that stage objective; beta=1 gives observed log likelihood. For beta different from one, stage improvement need not increase ordinary likelihood. Changing beta changes the optimized objective, so a cooling path is not ascent on a single unchanged likelihood surface.

The source’s high-temperature uniqueness and global-tracking argument is conditional, not a general convergence guarantee. On an unbounded continuous latent domain, the beta=0 uniform law need not exist and positive powers of a heavy-tailed density can have infinite normalizers. Negative log density also need not be nonnegative: normalized continuous densities can exceed one. Local warm-started optimization need not follow the global optimum through temperature changes or bifurcations.

Unique q maximizer is the actual posterior, and F then equals L. Theorem2 gives a joint local/global F maximum implies the corresponding L maximum, using posterior continuity for the local argument. Coordinatewise ascent, bounded iterates, attainment and convergence to a joint local maximum are separate requirements; an increasing F sequence alone is not a proof of all of them.

PDF6-8 Section3 Eq6-9: independent complete-data cases P(y,z|theta)=product_i P(y_i,z_i|theta), not arbitrary interacting latent coordinates. Cache each per-case distribution or expected sufficient statistic. Select a case, recompute its posterior under the current theta, leave other cases cached, then maximize the full cached complete-data expectation. For additive sufficient statistics, total_new=total_old-s_i_old+s_i_new. The M step uses the full cached total, not only the newly visited observation.

PDF7-8: updates can be cyclic or prefer unstabilized cases; minibatches of several cases are described. Fair revisiting and valid solves matter for fixed-point/convergence claims. claims.statement: For observations x with multiplicities n_x, finite latent states z, model parameters eta and a positive inverse temperature beta, minimize F_beta(q,eta)=sum_x n_x*sum_z q_xz*[log q_xz-beta*log p_eta(x,z)]. For fixed eta, on positive joint support use q_xz=p_eta(x,z)^beta/sum_j p_eta(x,j)^beta. For fixed q and beta>0, minimizing F_beta over eta is equivalent to maximizing the expected complete log likelihood; in PLSA this gives the usual normalized expected-count M-step with the tempered responsibilities. At beta=1 the E-step is the ordinary posterior. With 0<beta<1 it is flatter on its positive support. Hofmann’s inverse-annealing schedule first runs early-stopped EM at beta=1, then reduces beta multiplicatively, continues iterations while held-out performance improves, and stops decreasing beta when further improvements cease. At fixed beta, exact block updates optimize that temperature’s free energy; changing beta changes the objective.

native_neighbors.definition: A stochastic optimization procedure that explores candidate configurations with temperature-controlled acceptance of cost-increasing moves and progressively cools that acceptance process to concentrate search on low-cost configurations.
native_neighbors.identity_notes: This record denotes the temperature-scheduled optimization procedure exemplified by Kirkpatrick, Gelatt and Vecchi. Its basic symmetric-proposal Metropolis step is distinguished from fixed-temperature target sampling, generic annealing metaphors, training signal annealing and a proof that a particular finite schedule reaches a global minimum. The 1983 article is a primary formulation, not a claim of exclusive invention. limitations: The exp(−delta/T) expression is for positive effective temperature with the physical Boltzmann constant absorbed into its cost units. Zero temperature is a limiting or separately defined greedy rule, not evaluation of that quotient at T=0. Equal-cost moves are accepted in the displayed symmetric-proposal rule.

At fixed T the Boltzmann interpretation requires a proper target and a valid transition construction. Arbitrary asymmetric proposals do not justify dropping the reverse-to-forward proposal ratio. Lowering T changes the target; stationarity for a fixed stage does not imply equilibrium throughout a finite cooling run.

Positive-temperature uphill acceptance only permits escape through moves supported by the proposal. It does not ensure reaching every state, escaping a local basin in a chosen budget or tracking equilibrium. Rapid cooling can freeze search prematurely; schedule length, cost scale, move connectivity and constraints matter.

The primary article’s heuristics and empirical scaling claims are not a finite-run global-convergence theorem or a universal complexity bound. The estimator may be maximum likelihood, least squares or another supported complete-data estimator. limitations: The complete-data estimator must be defined on posterior-supported completed data and have the required moments. Empty mixture components, boundary or infinite MLEs, constrained parameter spaces and nonidentifiability need explicit conventions; a conditional mean can leave a nonconvex parameter space.

Conditional expectation is the least-squares approximation to an integrable squared-error target under a fixed law. That fact does not prove decreasing true parameter error, observed-likelihood monotonicity or global convergence across ICE iterations with changing laws.

The Delmas equivalence uses the mean/expectation parameter psi, although the source calls it canonical; its natural parameter phi is distinct. The claim is not automatic for arbitrary coordinates, curved/constrained exponential families or boundary estimates. A nonlinear transformation does not generally commute with conditional expectation.

For Gaussian mixtures, expectation of a complete-data class mean or variance containing a random class count differs in general from a ratio of expected sufficient statistics. The usual Gaussian-parameter ICE update therefore cannot simply be replaced by an EM update without checking the conditions.

Monte Carlo approximation requires valid posterior sampling and appropriate convergence conditions. Correlated Gibbs samples, finite sample counts and apparently steady parameters do not by themselves certify exact expectations or convergence. A one-sample version can resemble stochastic EM for a specific complete-data estimator; it is not every stochastic-approximation EM algorithm.

The inspected examples in Delmas contain scaling/covariance notation issues, and its introductory suggestion that mixed discrete-continuous data make likelihood irrelevant is not adopted. The definition and qualified coordinate comparison do not certify all printed example formulas. Neither inspected paper provides a universal empirical performance guarantee; no fitting, benchmark or author-code run was performed.
